findings.title: should_block? write clobbers the row and double-counts
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? loads a row, increments match_count in memory, and record.save writes every attribute back. That is last-write-wins with no row lock and no atomic UPDATE match_count = match_count + 1, so a concurrent admin change to action_type (for example switching block to do_nothing) can be overwritten by an in-flight check, and overlapping checks lose increments. The write also runs inside email validation, and UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, so one signup attempt runs the validator twice and adds 2 to match_count whenever any BlockedEmail row matches, including action_type do_nothing. A frequently submitted blocked address becomes a hot-row write on every attempt, and the new specs only call should_block? once so they still expect a +1 change.

findings.title: Blocked-email match is exact and case-sensitive
findings.body: should_block? uses BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first, and the unique index on blocked_emails.email is case-sensitive. Elsewhere this app canonicalizes addresses with Email.downcase and strip (UsersController#change_email) before comparing, but signup validation neither normalizes the submitted address nor the stored block row. A block for blocked@spam.com therefore does not match Blocked@spam.com, surrounding whitespace, or other case variants, and those addresses pass validation and can register. Uniqueness on BlockedEmail has the same comparison, so both casings can be stored as separate rows and .first still only sees an exact match.

findings.title: Domain allow/deny regex is not anchored
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? compiles Regexp.new("@(#{domains})") with no end anchor after only escaping dots. For a whitelist entry example.com, user@example.com.evil.com matches because @example.com is only required as a substring, so the address is treated as allowed and signup proceeds. The same helper is now the only domain check on User. Other regex metacharacters in the site setting are also unescaped, so a malformed domain list can raise RegexpError and 500 registration instead of failing validation.

findings.title: blocked_emails migration is not reflected in schema.rb
findings.body: This migration creates blocked_emails, but db/schema.rb is not updated. Discourse loads fresh and test databases from schema.rb (db:schema:load / db:test:prepare) rather than replaying every migration. New environments and CI will not have the table, so BlockedEmail.should_block? and the new specs will raise a missing-relation error until the schema dump is regenerated and committed.

findings.title: Any rejected email is shown as an invalid format
findings.body: On a failed create, any result.errors.email causes the submitted address to be pushed onto rejectedEmails. emailValidation then always fails with I18n.t('user.email.invalid'), the format-failure string, whether the server rejected a blocked address, a disallowed domain, or a duplicate. The new server string user.email.blocked is never shown on the field. The address also stays rejected for the life of the controller, so a transient 'already taken' failure cannot be retried without a full reload.

findings.title: Moved domain rules and block wiring are untested
findings.body: The EmailValidator examples stub BlockedEmail.should_block? and only check whether an error was added. They never set email_domains_whitelist or email_domains_blacklist, so the domain-restriction logic moved out of User#email_validator can break without a failing test. Nothing exercises User save or UsersController#create with a real BlockedEmail row, so a case-variant bypass or a double match_count increment on valid? plus save would also pass CI.
